episode_title: Where Has All the Infrastructure Gone?

stories.summary: When Ajay first came back to India, the entire country's connection to the internet was a single T1 line at the National Centre for Software Technology (NCST), led by S. Ramani. ERNET ran on 1.54 megabits per second for the whole country, and yet it seeded hundreds of individuals — Rajesh Jain, Shubham Mishra, Sanjay Jain — who would go on to power Indian computing.
stories.insight: A pittance of bandwidth, used well, can change a country's destiny. Knowledge spreads through small numbers of well-placed people; the seeding cost of a generation can be absurdly low if the right people get connected at the right moment.

stories.topic: Crawling Up the Coast — How Mphasis Built India's Services Map
stories.summary: The founder of Mphasis told Ajay they were 'crawling up the coast of Andhra Pradesh and Orissa, finding one city after another with a minimum population of five, ten lakh people.' They would put up a building, hire two thousand people, and be up and running. Call centres came first; English-correction and accent training did the rest.
stories.insight: Once the infrastructure (fiber optic cables) was built, services exports diffused organically across the entire country, not just metros. Services went where labour was cheap and English-trainable — exactly the theory the IT-ITES revolution was supposed to deliver, and did.

stories.topic: JNPT — Three Competing Terminals in One Port
stories.summary: JNPT in the 1990s was an example of magnificent policy: rather than handing the whole port to a single private bidder via PPP, the government organised it as three competing terminals — one government-run, two private. The government terminal helped establish cost benchmarks, while private competition kept everyone honest.
stories.insight: Good policy design can engineer competition where natural monopoly threatens. Sadly, Ajay notes, 'some of that level of brilliance in policy doesn't happen in many later episodes in Indian infrastructure.' The early 90s reformers were better policy designers than what came later.

stories.topic: Two Days at the Arvind Blue Jeans Factory
stories.summary: Ajay visited an Arvind Mills jeans manufacturing facility outside Bangalore — by their own claim the best in the country. 2,500 employees, world-class output, 100% exports. But the most interesting thing was the relentless mechanisation: because India's minimum wages and mandatory benefits are high, the factory keeps replacing humans with machines (e.g. a robot doing 'worsting' to give jeans the faded look) to stay competitive against Bangladesh and Vietnam. Day shifts are almost all women; 24-hour operations become 100% men due to safety, transport, and regulation.
stories.insight: A live demonstration of unintended consequences: minimum wage laws designed to help workers force factories to substitute capital for labour, eliminating jobs entirely. The choice for the worker becomes earning X or earning zero — and zero is worse. The Indian labour environment, not abstract economics, shapes the actual factory floor.

stories.topic: Sowmya Dhanaraj — From a Tea Stall on the Coimbatore Highway
stories.summary: Amit recalls his Seen and the Unseen episode with economist Sowmya Dhanaraj, whose father and mother were factory workers and whose mother sold tea for years at a stall on the Coimbatore Highway. Dhanaraj's research is on women in factories.
stories.insight: The best economists may be those who refuse to accept received wisdom from above and instead question everything on the basis of real-world experience. Lived poverty is not a disqualification for economic clarity — it is often a credential.

stories.summary: On a field trip, Ajay investigated the production of Lonavala chikki — the famous local sweet you can only buy in Lonavala. He asked a vendor whether they actually made it locally. The man answered: 'Of course we don't make it here; we make it in Ulhasnagar.' Amit jokes the label could read 'Made in USA — Ulhasnagar Sweets Association.'
stories.insight: A small, vivid demonstration of capitalism equalising differences. Real estate and labour in Lonavala are too expensive; production migrates to where input costs are low and the finished good comes back. The same logic that makes Bombay unable to host garment manufacturing makes Lonavala unable to host its own chikki.

recommendations.item: Young Rural Women in India Chase Big-City Dreams
recommendations.creator: Ellen Barry
recommendations.context: An NYT article on young women from rural Odisha relocating to Tirupur to work in low-end garment-export factories.
recommendations.reason: Ajay sees the emergence of firms and exports as 'the heart and soul of the Indian story,' but the data alone misses the human drama. Barry's article zooms in on the personal transformation — agency, choices, escape from village constraints — that even entry-level export jobs deliver to women.

recommendations.item: Follow-Up: A New Ending in Tale of Young Woman From Rural India
recommendations.creator: Ellen Barry
recommendations.context: Barry's follow-up piece tracking what happened next to one of the women in the original Tirupur story.
recommendations.reason: The continuation of the human-drama story — what becomes of one young rural woman after she has stepped into the export-led modern economy.

recommendations.item: The Odd Woman and the City
recommendations.creator: Vivian Gornick
recommendations.context: A memoir of a single woman's life and observations in New York City.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls Gornick's writing 'the best kind of writing — it just makes your brain explode.' He discovered the book while preparing show notes for his Loneliness of the Indian Woman episode and immediately fell in love. He and the team at the Beer studio have been reading paragraphs aloud to each other. Recommended as 'infrastructure for the mind' — the kind of book that makes you want to write.

recommendations.item: Sowmya Dhanaraj Is Making a Difference (Episode 380, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Sowmya Dhanaraj
recommendations.context: Amit's recent episode with the economist whose work focuses on women in factories.
recommendations.reason: Among Amit's top-ten favourite episodes. Dhanaraj's value is precisely that she questions received wisdom on the basis of lived working-class experience. Pairs with Ajay's Arvind Mills story as a window into the reality of Indian women's factory work.

recommendations.item: The Loneliness of the Indian Woman (Episode 259, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shrayana Bhattacharya
recommendations.context: Amit's most popular Seen and the Unseen episode to date.
recommendations.reason: The episode whose show-notes prep led Amit to discover Vivian Gornick — and a wider window into the inner lives of Indian women that connects to the Tirupur and factory-worker themes here.

recommendations.item: Where Has All the Education Gone?
recommendations.creator: Lant Pritchett
recommendations.context: Pritchett's seminal paper showing the global expansion of schooling years has not delivered the expected gains in development outcomes.
recommendations.reason: The model for this episode's argument: 'where has all the infrastructure gone?' borrows directly from Pritchett's framing. When you pile in inputs and the outputs don't follow, the right response is skepticism, diagnosis, and the courage to pull back funding until you understand the choke point.

recommendations.creator: Paul Graham
recommendations.context: Graham's essay categorising people on independent-vs-conventional and passive-vs-aggressive axes.
recommendations.reason: Amit references the 'aggressively conventional-minded' as the source of pushback whenever someone tries to update an inherited assumption — exactly the social barrier Ajay is fighting against in re-examining the infrastructure consensus.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's book on economic policy.
recommendations.reason: Source of the 'one rupee of government spending costs three rupees to GDP' argument, which Amit invokes to insist that even infrastructure spending must clear a high cost-benefit bar — not be assumed virtuous.

recommendations.item: That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen
recommendations.creator: Frederic Bastiat
recommendations.context: Bastiat's classic 1850 essay on opportunity cost and the unseen consequences of public spending.
recommendations.reason: The conceptual scaffolding for Amit's whole 'army of people digging ditches' argument against counting state spending as GDP. Bastiat is the foundational text for any honest analysis of what infrastructure money actually buys versus what it forecloses.

recommendations.item: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Episode 33 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's earlier full episode on public choice theory.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it an episode every Indian must watch. It supplies the framing for understanding why politicians announce ribbon-cutting projects rather than do humdrum maintenance, and why constituency-bound roads-to-nowhere are inevitable in the late stages of an infrastructure programme.

recommendations.item: A Deep Dive Into Education (Episode 54 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The previous EIE episode, which examined Lant Pritchett's argument that piling up years of schooling has not delivered development outcomes.
recommendations.reason: This infrastructure episode is the parallel argument: input piling without output progress demands a paradigm rethink, not more input.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of Chess (Episode 52 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.reason: Amit cites it as an example of a synthesis episode — bringing together what he already knew with enthusiasm — versus the present episode which contains genuinely novel claims about Indian infrastructure.

recommendations.item: How Family Firms Evolve (Episode 34 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.reason: Linked in the show notes as part of the firms-and-internationalisation strand of EIE that grounds Ajay's claim that 50%+ of global trade happens intra-firm and that the host-MNC theory is the engine of development.

recommendations.item: From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Episode 37 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's episode on the evolution of firm types.
recommendations.reason: Part of the firms strand of EIE, supporting the argument that India's growth strategy depends on becoming a host to global value chains.

recommendations.item: Graduating to Globalisation (Episode 48 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.reason: Linked as background reading for the globalisation-of-production framework underlying Ajay's argument that the goods exports failure is the most important fact about contemporary Indian development.

recommendations.item: The Long Road to Change (Episode 36 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's earlier episode on policy change.
recommendations.reason: Linked in the show notes as part of the broader policy-process literature underlying Ajay's call to 'walk the policy pipeline' — data, research, debate, expert reports, laws, implementation — for government contracting.

recommendations.creator: XKDR Forum
recommendations.context: XKDR Forum's research programme on public finance and government contracting.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's organisation is running 'a vibrant research program on how to do government contracting better.' He flags this as a high-priority frontier — building state capability for contracting is what's missing in the post-PPP retreat.

core_ideas.explanation: If there is a difference in wages or real-estate costs between two places, capitalism creates a business opportunity to arbitrage that gap — produce in the cheap location, ferry the result to the expensive one. You make chikki in Ulhasnagar and sell in Lonavala. You don't put a garment factory in Bombay because wages and rent are too high. The grand theory of Indian development is that infrastructure is what allows capitalism to equalise differences across the country, locating production in remote, low-wage India.
core_ideas.quote: Capitalism works by equalising differences. So if there's a difference in a wage, there's a business opportunity.

core_ideas.concept: The Goods Exports Failure (Where Has All the Infrastructure Gone?)
core_ideas.explanation: Over the ten-year period FY2012-13 to FY2022-23 — a period chosen to flatter India because it includes the post-COVID rich-country goods import surge — Indian goods exports grew at just 4% nominal in US dollars, or about 1.3% in real dollars after subtracting US inflation of ~2.7%. At that rate, exports double every 52-56 years. Despite enormous investment in container ports, highways, airports, and railways, the manufacturing exports revolution that infrastructure was supposed to enable has simply not happened. FDI growth tells the same story (~4% real). The original 1990s theory — that infrastructure would let global value chains locate production in remote, low-wage India — has not delivered for goods.
core_ideas.quote: I'd like to say where has all the infrastructure gone? It isn't working. We are not getting that goods exports revolution.

core_ideas.explanation: The technical lens for asking whether more capital is buying more output. Not stocks, but flows: how much extra GDP comes from an extra rupee of investment. The ICOR for infrastructure was great in the 1990s; for goods-export-oriented infrastructure today it has collapsed. Ajay catalogues four reasons: (1) diminishing marginal returns — the best projects are done first; (2) the retreat from PPP back to direct government building, which raises construction cost and worsens operations and maintenance; (3) projects becoming political — placed in powerful constituencies or near religious sites rather than where economic returns lie; (4) public-choice incentives — politicians love announcements and ribbons but loathe the unglamorous regulation and maintenance work afterward.

core_ideas.concept: Services Worked Because the State Got Out of the Way
core_ideas.explanation: The IT-ITES revolution didn't need a huge programme of public spending — it needed the state to stop owning telecom. The 1999 Vajpayee-era reform (driven by Sudhindra Kulkarni and N. K. Singh) broke the Department of Telecom's stranglehold and the VSNL monopoly on international telephony. The private sector then ran fiber optic cables to India on its own dime — landing stations from the Middle East to Bombay, from Madras to Singapore — and India suddenly had infinite bandwidth. No public capex, just user charges. That is the cleanest infrastructure success story India has, and it came from withdrawal, not investment.
core_ideas.quote: You don't need government money. You just need user charges.

core_ideas.concept: Goods Infrastructure Did Not Deliver The Way Services Infrastructure Did
core_ideas.explanation: Ports, container terminals, highways, airports, railways were all built — JNPT, Kandla, the Golden Quadrilateral, NHAI highways — and the bang for the buck was nowhere near what fiber optics delivered. The asymmetry is the central puzzle of the episode: the same theory of change worked for one stream of production and not the other. The data demands we ask why — and resist the temptation to blame infrastructure shortfalls and spend more.

core_ideas.concept: Viability Gap Funding (How PPPs Were Supposed to Stay Honest)
core_ideas.explanation: Ashok Lahiri's clever construct in the Ministry of Finance: when externalities mean a road's user charges alone won't pay for it, the government announces the project and runs a reverse auction — private bidders compete on how little subsidy they will accept. Once the subsidy is fixed, the private builder bears the rest of the risk and has every incentive to control cost and run the asset well. The mechanism preserves the PPP discipline (private capital does sanity checks; the private sector won't sign on to a true road-to-nowhere) while still funding genuine externalities. India built up this capability and then, when contracting got hard, walked away.

core_ideas.concept: The Retreat From PPP Was a Failure of Imagination, Not a Verdict on PPP
core_ideas.explanation: When early PPP infrastructure ran into contracting failures, the right response was deeper research into government contracting as a core state capability — the same way you walk the policy pipeline of data, research, rival proposals, public debate, expert committees, laws, implementation. Instead, the Indian state retreated to direct government construction. The result: more expensive assets, worse maintenance, more politicised project selection, more ribbon-cutting and less regulation. The state walked away from the hard problem.

China's massive central-planned infrastructure build-out wasted trillions of dollars of poor people's hard-earned money on assets nobody needed. Roads were built where there was nothing at the other end. In the short run everyone is happy — construction contracts, ribbons, GDP numbers — but at the deeper economic level, the ICOR collapses. We already know China was wrong; the question is whether India is following the same path on a smaller scale.

core_ideas.concept: The Binding Constraint May Have Moved
core_ideas.explanation: The right framework is to ask: at this moment, what is the choke point? What is the binding constraint on the emergence of globalised firms in India? Ajay's hypothesis is that in 2024 it is no longer infrastructure — it is more likely capital controls, taxation rules tormenting foreign firms, and other operational obstacles to FDI and global value chain participation. Once those are fixed and FDI starts surging, infrastructure may quickly become the binding constraint again, and at that point we should rotate back into building. But not before. Don't pile money on a non-binding constraint.
core_ideas.quote: Infrastructure is probably not the binding constraint today.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's universalisation of Ajay's PPP-retreat point: institutions and individuals tend to walk away from genuinely hard problems and pick easy answers. Government contracting is hard, so the state went back to building things itself. Infrastructure regulation is hard, so it became toothless. Development economics often runs from its hardest questions for the same reason. The lesson: the value is precisely where the hard questions are. Don't reach for a convenient frame just because it's easy to act on.

Ajay's classification scheme. The first barrier is social — conventional wisdom, the views of famous people and Nobel laureates, the views of one's tribe — which interferes with most people. Ajay claims he is naturally immune to this since childhood: he treats every famous opinion as a kick-off for argument, never reverence. The second barrier is arrogance: once you have figured something out, the temptation to refuse to update. This one is harder; even Keynes's 'when the facts change, I change my mind' is something most people, including Ajay, do too slowly. The endless work of intellectual life is bayesian updating that is faster than your ego allows.
core_ideas.quote: When the facts change, I change my mind. What do you do, sir?

core_ideas.concept: Minimum Wage as Capital-for-Labour Substitution Engine
core_ideas.explanation: The Arvind Mills factory shows the unseen consequence of high minimum wages and mandatory benefits in India: factories invest constantly in machines to replace workers. A robot does the worsting that a person used to do. Each capital-investment decision is a hard-nosed internal-rate-of-return calculation, and one by one the machines arrive. The worker is not paid more; the worker is removed from the line. The minimum wage that was meant to help workers ends up making it more profitable to replace them — and against Bangladesh and Vietnam, the alternative is bankruptcy.

core_ideas.concept: Government Spending in GDP — A Conceptual Mistake
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's foundational quarrel with national-accounting orthodoxy. If the state hired an army to dig ditches and fill them in, GDP would rise. The flaw is that government expenditure goes in 'plus' without any test of whether the spending creates value. The same money in private hands is also being spent — into the economy — but on things people actually want. Bastiat's framing of the seen and the unseen is the corrective: every rupee of state spending has an enormous opportunity cost that vanishes in headline GDP.

core_ideas.concept: One Rupee of Government Spending Costs Three Rupees of GDP
core_ideas.explanation: From Kelkar and Shah's In Service of the Republic. The cost is not just the rupee taken — it is the deadweight loss of the coercion (taxation distortion, compliance burden, opportunity cost, moral cost). Every state spending decision must clear a high bar: a 1-to-1 cost-benefit test radically understates the social cost. This is why even apparently virtuous infrastructure spending must be put on trial.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit and Ajay's running self-description: 'We have uncle and auntie, leaving Dad aside.' Beer-sessions setting in the hills, with the implication they may never come back to the plains.

Amit notices an ant climbing up Ajay's pristine white kurta during the introduction — 'the Sanskari look' — and Ajay calmly continues philosophising while the ant advances. Ajay later replies he has anthropomorphised the block named infrastructure and trying to climb the policy table.
Lonavala chikki is actually made in Ulhasnagar. Amit's punchline: 'You could actually write on it Made in USA — USA standing for Ulhasnagar Sweets Association.'
On the inevitability of self-deprecation in disagreement: 'Puny little me is going to argue about this with a great person?' — Ajay's framing of his stance toward Larry Summers and Marty Feldstein.

Amit's mock-economic argument against fellow public spending: 'You could have an army of people digging up ditches, filling them up, digging up ditches, filling them up, rinse and repeat — and the GDP just keeps going up.'
John Maynard Keynes (apocryphally): 'When the facts change, I change my mind. What do you do, sir?' — Ajay's standard for bayesian updating, and his admission that he himself does it too slowly.
Paul Graham's 'aggressively conventional-minded' from The Four Quadrants of Conformism — Amit invokes the phrase to describe the tribal pushback against re-examined assumptions.
Frederic Bastiat's 'That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen' — the conceptual root of Amit's opportunity-cost critique of state spending in GDP.
Lant Pritchett's 'Where Has All the Education Gone?' — the title and methodology that this episode borrows for its central question about infrastructure.

The 1999 Vajpayee-era telecom reform, attributed by Ajay to Sudhindra Kulkarni and N. K. Singh: 'one of the most important moments of the Indian economic reforms,' breaking the VSNL monopoly on international telephony.

The phrase 'fax-mille copies of those arguments' — Ajay's swipe at how the same statist arguments once used to defend the VSNL monopoly are now used in other sectors. The 'fax' pun underscores how dated the thinking is.

S. Ramani and ERNET — the National Centre for Software Technology team who ran India's entire internet on a single 1.54 Mbps T1 line in the early 1990s. Among the seeded generation: Rajesh Jain, Shubham Mishra, Sanjay Jain.

Ashok Lahiri's Viability Gap Funding — the reverse-auction PPP construct from the Ministry of Finance designed to overcome the externalities-vs-user-charges problem in road and infrastructure projects.
